transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-04-25
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 34 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Alice Tran (Redwood AE), Marcus Li (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (CTO - Zenith), Evan Cole (Platform Lead), Maria Gonzales (Compliance)
Recording: https://zoom.example/recording/ff-20260425

Summary: quick sync to understand production availability requirements and map Redwood hosting options (Hosted / Dedicated / Private) to their risk appetite.

Topics: SLA targets, multi-region routing, fallback strategies, audit/KMS, benchmarking plan.

Transcript:
[00:00] Alice (Redwood AE): okay good afternoon everyone, thanks for making time, i'm alice from redwood, i'll kick off, we've got marcus with me from the se team.  how's everyone doing?
[00:08] Priya (CTO): doing great, thanks. we've got a hard requirement to map out availability before our next architecture review, so wanted to use this slot for that.
[00:15] Marcus (Redwood SE): hi all, quick agenda — understand current infra, desired sles and sros, failure scenarios, and then propose routing / fallback options and pilot plan. sound good?
[00:24] Evan (Platform Lead): yep, that's exactly it. our key question: can we get to a 99.95% user-facing SLA for real-time assistant calls with latencies under 250ms p95?
[00:35] Alice: good — and just so we set expectations, 99.95 across live text generation is a tough SLO when you need sub-250ms p95, depends a lot on model size, region, and whether you want dedicated capacity. we can break down tradeoffs.
[00:47] Maria (Compliance): and for us we need SOC2 compliance, audit logs for all key operations, and keys stored in our KMS. also data residency constraints — we must keep EU customer data in eu cloud region.
[01:00] Alice: understood, we support customer-managed KMS for Dedicated and Private, and we can lock region routing. we'll share SOC2 and ISO docs after the call.
[01:09] Priya: great. can you talk through how your fallback policies work if an instance/region goes offline? we can't have silent failures or long retries that surface bad UX.
[01:18] Marcus: sure — at a high level we support policy-driven routing. simplest is active-primary region with cold-standby in secondary, warm replicas with mirroring of model cache to reduce warmup. alternative is active-active multi-region, which gives lower failover but higher cost. also we have automatic variant fallback to quantized model to preserve latency.
[01:36] Evan: when you say automatic variant fallback, is that real-time? we cannot have the assistant slow down by several seconds while we swap models.
[01:44] Marcus: correct, the runtime can route to a compatible variant in the same region or a nearby region, and if KV cache is unavailable we'll rehydrate — which causes a short latency spike on the first request. we mitigate by prefix caching and pro-active background pre-warm if you enable reserved capacity.
[02:01] Priya: what's the typical RTO for a regional outage if we use Dedicated pools in two regions?
[02:06] Marcus: with warm replicas and network-level routing, we've seen RTOs under 30s for most outages, but full stateful cache rehydration can take a few minutes for large context lengths; the user-facing impact is usually a p95 latency spike for a rolling window.
[02:21] Alice: if the requirement is strict 250ms p95, we'd recommend Dedicated capacity in both regions + intelligent routing at the edge to keep traffic local and failover traffic gradually. This bumps cost but hits the SLO.
[02:36] Evan: how about Hosted? can hosted meet 99.9 with the latency we want?
[02:41] Marcus: Hosted can meet 99.9 in many cases, and we provision pools by model popularity, but because it's multi-tenant we cannot guarantee region-isolated reserved GPUs unless you move to Dedicated. if you need strict data residency and KMS control, Hosted is not the right fit.
[02:56] Maria: on the audit side, we need immutable logs of model version used per request and who accessed keys. can you provide that?
[03:03] Alice: yes, audit trails per token/request are available — for Private and Dedicated we can forward logs to your SIEM and include model metadata. we'll include an example schema in the docs.
[03:12] Priya: ok, another operational question — in incident scenarios do you do automatic throttling or shed low-priority traffic first? we have some internal batch tasks that could be deprioritized.
[03:22] Marcus: we support policy layers: route by traffic class, and we can apply backpressure to non-critical routes or synthetic jobs. customers can define priority labels and we expose metrics to tune this.
[03:31] Evan: what about rollback and canary? if a rollout causes regression we can't have a global impact.
[03:36] Alice: rollouts support canary percentages and auto-fallback to previous model variant on error thresholds. for Dedicated customers we also support traffic-splitting across versions and automatic regression alerts tied to eval prompts.
[03:48] Priya: for our compliance team, what's the timeline on Private deployment? on-prem is preferred for some regulated flows.
[03:55] Marcus: Private (VPC or on-prem) typically takes 6-10 weeks depending on network approvals and HSM integration; shorter if you accept our VPC package. full air-gapped on-prem is the longest due to hardware validation.
[04:07] Maria: HSM integration — we need to ensure key access logs are retained 7 years and key rotation policies fit our cert.
[04:14] Alice: noted — we have KMS/HSM integrations with audit forwarding; we'll share policy templates.
[04:19] Evan: let's talk incident tolerance in more concrete terms. assume primary region us-east goes down. what happens to in-flight requests and queued requests?
[04:27] Marcus: in-flight requests to instances that die will return errors; our edge layer retries according to policy with exponential backoff and will route to secondary region. we do not transparently replay partial tokens — clients should expect some failed requests and implement at-least-once or idempotency where possible. queued requests in our admission controller can be drained to secondary if capacity exists.
[04:46] Priya: so there is potential for duplicate completion if retry isn't idempotent — good to know. we'll need guidance for our engineers.
[04:53] Alice: we'll provide a retry/Idempotency guide.
[04:56] Evan: cost — what's the hit if we do active-active across two regions for Dedicated? rough ballpark.
[05:01] Alice: roughly 1.6–2x cost depending on idle utilization and cache locality; dual dedicated pools plus cross-region replication add overhead. Marcus can follow up with more exact numbers once we see your qps profile.
[05:13] Marcus: yeah, send us the sample workload and we'll model it; the benchmark will include token/sec, average request size, p95 latency targets so we can propose pre-warm sizing.
[05:22] Priya: we'll share a traffic spreadsheet and a sample anonymized dataset. Maria: data classification - we have PII in some prompts, so encryption at rest and in transit plus a bounded retention policy is mandatory.
[05:33] Alice: for PII we recommend Private or Dedicated with customer-managed keys and strict retention. Hosted can be configured but not ideal for long-term PII retention.
[05:42] Maria: okay. another concern: how do you surface partial outages? our ops team needs an alerting contract — do you integrate with pagerduty and produce recovery timelines?
[05:51] Marcus: yes, Redwood Console integrates with PagerDuty, Datadog, and we export incident metrics and SLO burn rates. For Dedicated/Private customers we provide a dedicated support channel and an SLA playbook with RTO/RPO targets.
[06:03] Priya: can we see example runbooks?
[06:06] Alice: yes we'll share a sample operational playbook and can tailor it during the pilot.
[06:10] Evan: any limitations on model size for multi-region replication? if we have a large 70B family model, does that increase failover time?
[06:18] Marcus: larger models mean larger KV caches and longer rehydration. we can mitigate by quantized variants, sharded weights across GPUs, and prefix caching. replication still takes time but active-active avoids rehydration.
[06:29] Priya: what's your recommendation for us — we run high-sensitivity financial assistant, medium qps (about 120 requests per second peak) with average context 1k tokens.
[06:40] Marcus: for 120 rps at 1k context and 250ms p95, we'd recommend Dedicated with reserved pools in primary region and a warm standby in secondary, plus edge routing to keep EU traffic in eu for residency. active-active if budget allows.
[06:55] Alice: and for the pilot we can do a 2-week Dedicated trial in a single region to prove p95 latency and cost per 1M tokens; then expand to a second region for availability testing.
[07:06] Evan: how long to stand up a Dedicated pilot?
[07:09] Marcus: usually 1–2 weeks for provisioning a Dedicated pool and baseline integration, assuming no special networking approvals. with VPC peering or on-prem it takes longer.
[07:18] Priya: ok that's helpful. now about the SLA language — we need explicit credits and definitions for downtime and partial degradation. do you have a standard 99.9/99.95 table?
[07:28] Alice: yes, our contract templates include uptime definitions, measurement windows, and credit tables. we'll share examples; note that 99.95 for interactive generation will assume reserved capacity and cross-region redundancy.
[07:40] Maria: can you also add clauses for data residency and key custody in the draft?
[07:44] Alice: absolutely. we'll flag those in the template and suggest Private for stricter requirements.
[07:49] Evan: one last technical — when routing to secondary region do you support geo-proximity routing vs. weighted failover?
[07:55] Marcus: both. our smart routing supports latency-based geo-proximity, and you can also configure weighted failover windows and gradual traffic shifting to avoid cold-start storms.
[08:06] Priya: what about consistency for stateful sessions — if we route a user to another region mid-session, how are session contexts handled?
[08:14] Marcus: good question — session affinity is best effort; for long-lived context we recommend storing session KV in a replicated store accessible by both regions or use an explicit session handoff mechanism. otherwise you'll see partial history unless you replicate cache.
[08:28] Priya: we'll need to evaluate that for our conversational flows.
[08:31] Maria: compliance follow-up — please include retention and deletion workflow for request logs; we need proof for audits.
[08:37] Alice: will do.
[08:39] Evan: what's the mechanism for emergency capacity in case of traffic spikes? can you burst into other regions or add temporary nodes?
[08:47] Marcus: Dedicated has burst policies and autoscaling; we also offer short-term burst credits and the ability to spin up extra capacity in adjacent regions if quotas are available. Hosted can also burst but with less predictability.
[08:58] Priya: for the benchmark, can you instrument our end-to-end latency including network hops? we want the client-to-token time measured.
[09:06] Marcus: yes, our benchmark harness measures client-to-token, kernel latencies, and reports p50/p95/p99. we'll include telemetry hooks for your APM.
[09:15] Alice: quick operational note — we'll need a short infra contact list, network CIDRs for peering, and sample keys for HSM mock to do initial validation.
[09:25] Evan: i'll circulate network details after this call.
[09:28] Priya: are there known edge cases where failover could cause data to leave the region briefly? we need guarantees for EU residency especially.
[09:36] Marcus: if you configure strict residency routing, we avoid routing EU-backed requests to non-EU by default; fallback to non-EU only happens if you allow cross-region fallback in policy. we can also keep a cold standby in eu to avoid cross-border movement.
[09:49] Maria: good. one more — do you provide SLA reports monthly and have an escalation path for breaches?
[09:56] Alice: yes, monthly SLO reports and a designated escalation engineer for Dedicated customers, plus credits per contract.
[10:03] Evan: ok, let's talk timeline: can you send pricing and SOC docs by Friday?
[10:08] Alice: yes, we'll send by Friday and propose benchmark slot for week of May 4.
[10:13] Priya: agreed.
[10:15] Maria: thanks, this was productive.
[10:18] Marcus: before we wrap — i'll attach an operational playbook and a sample benchmark plan in the follow-up.
[10:24] Alice: great. recap of next steps: we'll send pricing and contract templates, SOC docs, and a benchmark plan. customer to send traffic spreadsheet and network info.
[10:33] Evan: thanks everyone.
[10:35] Priya: thanks.
[10:36] Meeting end.

Notes on quality: some transcription artifacts are present — names and acronyms occasionally misrecognized (e.g., HSM vs. HSMN), filler words retained.
